aeo-rankings-to-citations.body_text: AEO: the shift from keyword rankings to citation tracking | Inflexion AI Discovery / AEO AEO: the shift from keyword rankings to citation tracking Search is no longer about ranking for keywords. It is about being cited in AI answers. Here is how the measurement model is changing. 19 September 2026 · 10 min read · Inflexion journal On this page 01 / The old model 02 / The new model 03 / What measurement looks like now 04 / Different engines, different signals 05 / What this means for your strategy For two decades, the SEO playbook was stable. Rank for keywords. Drive traffic. Convert visitors. The metric that mattered was position one through ten. That model is breaking. Not because SEO stopped working. Because the surface where discovery happens has shifted. Semrush projects that LLM referral traffic will overtake traditional Google search by the end of 2027. In the past three months alone, LLM referrals grew 800 percent year over year. Google AI Overviews now appear on billions of searches monthly, covering at least 13 percent of all SERPs. The surface has changed. The measurement has not caught up. 01. The old model was built for clicks. The new model is built for citations. The old question: where do we rank for this keyword? The new question: does the model cite us when someone asks this question? They are not the same. A page ranking position three for a keyword may be absent from the AI answer to the same query. We have measured this gap across dozens of categories. It is larger than most marketing teams realise. AI Overviews and chatbots do not simply read the top ten results. They retrieve from a wider index, weight authority differently, and prefer content structured for direct extraction. The metric that matters is not position. It is share of answer. How often does your brand appear in the generated response? At what position within the answer? With what sentiment? Ranking is a proxy for visibility. Citation is visibility itself. 02. The signals have changed. The playbook has not caught up. Traditional SEO measures keyword density, backlink volume, page speed, and technical crawlability. AEO uses different signals. Authority now means how often other trusted sources cite you. Backlinks still matter. But unlinked brand mentions across Reddit, Wikipedia, YouTube, industry forums, and news outlets now carry weight. LLMs read the text around your brand name. They do not require a hyperlink to register the association. Relevance means whether your content directly answers the question being asked. Keyword density matters less than factual clarity. A clear, direct answer in the first paragraph of a page outweighs keyword-stuffed content that buries the answer. Clarity means whether the model can parse your content. Structure matters. Schema markup, FAQ format, clear headings, and extractable answers help the model retrieve and cite you. Pages with quotes or statistics have been shown to have 30 to 40 percent higher visibility in AI answers. Freshness means how recent your content is. LLMs have a clear preference for recent content. Content audits are non-negotiable. Update statistics, screenshots, and examples. Remove references to outdated tools. Add new sections covering recent developments. The old playbook: keyword density, backlink volume, page speed. The new playbook: authority mentions, direct answers, extractable structure, content freshness. 03. Measurement has moved from rankings to share of answer. You cannot improve what you do not measure. The old dashboard showed keyword rankings, organic traffic, and click-through rate. The new dashboard needs different metrics. Share of answer: the proportion of a defined buyer prompt set, across a defined set of models, in which your brand appears in the generated answer. Position within the answer is recorded. Being named as the first recommendation is different from being mentioned in a list of three. Citation sources: when a model names a competitor, trace what it drew from. Independent reviews, comparison tables, analyst reports, forum discussions. The source map tells you exactly where to build credibility. Sentiment and framing: is your brand recommended positively, mentioned neutrally, or described with caveats? Models do not express opinions, but their wording frames brands differently. A brand described as "a leading provider" competes differently from one described as "also offers." Cross-model consistency: models disagree. A brand well-cited in Claude can be absent from GPT. The 11 percent domain overlap between ChatGPT and Perplexity proves it. You need visibility across the models your buyers actually use. The prompt set is fixed and published. The number means something because the questions did not change. 04. Different engines, different signals. One strategy does not transfer. ChatGPT favors credible, authoritative sources with clear entity signals. Comparison content has a 95 percent citation rate. Documentation and resources hit 86 percent. Google Gemini pulls heavily from pages that already perform well organically, typically within the top 20 results. Blog content performs particularly well in AI Overviews at 42 percent citation rate. Perplexity cites well-researched, comprehensive content that combines multiple perspectives. Academic sources and data-driven content perform well. Blog posts and informative articles hit 80 percent citation rate. Copilot favors content that clearly states what a product or service does, includes pricing or comparison information, and has strong brand signals. The strategy shifts by target engine. A single approach does not transfer. You need to know which engines your buyers use and match their specific retrieval logic. 05. What this means for your strategy. The shift is not optional. On Marketing's October 2025 survey found that 37 percent of marketing teams are already actively optimising for AI search. Another 30 percent are exploring it. Eighty percent plan to have AI search strategies in place within a year. The teams that start tracking now will have the baseline when the market catches up. The teams that wait will be measuring from zero. Start with a pilot. Map 5 to 10 high-priority buyer questions. Test across ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, and Google AI Overviews. Record where you appear, where competitors appear, and where nobody does. That baseline document is yours to keep. Then build the system: prompt mapping, citation tracking, source authority mapping, content built for citation. Track monthly against the fixed prompt set. The number means something because the questions did not change. AEO does not replace SEO. Strong SEO fuels AEO. AI systems favour content from trusted domains with strong organic rankings. But the measurement model has shifted. The teams that understand the new metrics will make better decisions. The teams that keep reporting keyword rankings will be reporting on a surface that matters less every quarter. agentic-media-buying.body_text: Agentic media buying: from dashboards to autonomous execution | Inflexion Media / Agentic AI Agentic media buying: from dashboards to autonomous execution AI agents are replacing channel-by-channel media buying with portfolio-based coordination. The shift from dashboard-driven management to continuous execution. 19 September 2026 · 9 min read · Inflexion journal On this page 01 / The dashboard problem 02 / What agents actually do 03 / The infrastructure shift 04 / Governance in an agentic world For years, media buying has been dashboard-driven. Teams pull reports. Interpret what happened. Make decisions. Execute changes. Wait for the next report. The cycle is monthly at best, weekly at most. Agentic AI changes the cycle time. CommerceIQ's Ally AI agents now handle repetitive, high-volume operational tasks across sales, digital shelf, content, and retail media. The platform deploys agents for Shelf, Media, Sales, and Content. Media agents improve retail media performance using 50-plus retail signals at 40 times the scale of traditional rules-based campaign management. The shift is structural. Retail teams manage thousands of SKUs, optimize content, run retail media, and manage pricing and inventory across multiple retailers. Human teams cannot keep up. Currently, most teams spend much of their time pulling reports to interpret what happened. AI becomes valuable when it can understand the why and take immediate action. 01. The dashboard problem. Dashboards show what happened. They do not show what to do. A human reads the dashboard, forms a hypothesis, decides on an action, and executes it. The latency between insight and action is measured in days or weeks. Meanwhile, the algorithmic environment moves in real time. Bids adjust. Budgets pace. Competitors react. Inventory changes. The dashboard is always describing a past state. Scope3 describes the future as agent-to-agent media buying: AI agents replacing channel-by-channel media buying with portfolio-based coordination. The Unified Context Protocol, Advertising Context Protocol, and Agentic RTB Framework give AI agents a shared framework to communicate and collaborate. Early pilots are underway. Butler/Till is testing a media activation agent with Scope3, targeting a 40 percent cost reduction in media plan execution. The economics are shifting from human-operated dashboards to agent-operated execution. The dashboard describes the past. The agent acts in the present. 02. What agents actually do. Current genAI tools generate copy, suggest bids, and surface insights. Agentic AI is different. It is defined by independent decision-making, goal-oriented behaviour, and complex task execution without continuous human input. CommerceIQ's Ally AI agents demonstrate the pattern: Shelf Agent monitors content, availability, assortment, reviews, and search (CAARS) to create branded insight packs with recommended actions in seconds. Media Agent improves retail media performance using 50-plus retail signals at 40 times the scale of traditional rules-based campaign management. Retail media agents execute thousands of changes per day compared to the limited volume typical of manual or agency-led workflows. Sales Agent and Content Agent handle their respective domains with the same pattern: continuous monitoring, hypothesis generation, and autonomous execution within defined guardrails. The agents connect content, retail media, search, inventory, and demand data across systems. They do not just report on the data. They act on it. 03. The infrastructure shift. Agentic media buying requires new infrastructure. EMARKETER notes that the Unified Context Protocol (UCP), Advertising Context Protocol (AdCP), and Agentic RTB Framework (ARTF) give AI agents a shared framework to communicate and collaborate. This is not a feature upgrade. It is a system-level rebuild. Five shifts the industry is making in 2026: From channel-by-channel to portfolio-based coordination. From human-paced to real-time decisioning. From rules-based to goal-oriented control. From dashboard-driven to agent-driven execution. From siloed data to unified context. The first deliverable on every engagement is now a clean, unified data layer that every channel reads from. Most brands have seven disconnected tools producing conflicting signals. The first deliverable is a clean, unified data layer that every channel reads from. Clean first-party data is the fuel. Agentic AI is the engine. The work that matters is feeding the engine the right signals and defining what it should prioritise. The infrastructure is not the platform. The infrastructure is the data layer the agents share. 04. Governance in an agentic world. Nearly 80 percent of retail teams say they are open to reallocating agency budgets to AI agents if recommendations are transparent and human teams retain final control. The governance model must evolve. From human approval of every decision to human approval of the objective function. The agent works within the objective function. The human sets the objective function: target ROAS, budget caps, brand safety constraints, inventory constraints. From monthly reviews to continuous monitoring. The agent executes thousands of changes per day. The human reviews the outcome patterns weekly and adjusts the objective function monthly. From agency-managed to brand-owned with agent support. The brand owns the data, the objective function, and the guardrails. The agent executes. The agency advises on strategy and objective function design. Transparency is the prerequisite. The agent must log every decision, the signal that triggered it, the expected outcome, and the actual outcome. The human team audits the log. The system learns from the audit. CommerceIQ's CEO Guru Hariharan frames it: "Retail is moving faster than human teams can keep up with. AI becomes truly valuable when it can understand the why and take immediate action. That is the shift to Agentic Commerce." Sources Scope3, How AI agents work in media buying and programmatic , August 2025. Scope3, What Is Agent-to-Agent Media Buying? , February 2026. The real mechanics How AI models decide who to cite: and what that means for your content strategy. When a user asks a model a question, the model does not search Google and read the top result. It generates an answer from its training data and, where retrieval is available, draws on external sources. Models reward four things: authority (how often a source is cited by other sources the model trusts), relevance (whether the content directly answers the question being asked), clarity (whether the information is structured so the model can parse it), and freshness (how recent the content is). There is no position one through ten. There is being in the answer and not being in the answer . Brands that rank first on Google for a query are often absent from the AI answer to the same query, because models and search engines weigh signals differently. We have measured this gap across dozens of categories. It is larger than most marketing teams realise. This is why traditional SEO, built around keyword ranking, backlink volume and click-through rate, does not translate directly to AI citation. The work is adjacent but distinct. The skills overlap but the output metric is different. Some AEO services largely reproduce traditional SEO. The actual work is about being the clearest, most authoritative source on a specific question , not about filling a keyword gap. 02. The audit What we actually check when we check your AI visibility. Nobody can plan this without a baseline, and almost nobody has one. The diagnostic is deliberately specified tightly enough that you could commission it from someone else. The diagnostic includes an operational reading of the output and a plan that follows from it. 01 Prompt set construction. We build a set of buyer questions specific to your category, covering the arc from broad category awareness through to comparison and purchase-intent queries. We exclude brand-name searches: nobody discovers you by typing your name. The prompt set is published to you and fixed for the duration of the engagement. 02 Cross-model testing. The same prompt set run across four to six models, depending on what your buyers actually use. Models disagree more than expected: a brand well-cited in Claude can be absent from GPT, and neither pattern predicts Gemini or Perplexity. Testing one model gives a misleading picture. 03 Source mapping. When a model names a competitor, we trace what it drew from. This reveals which sources carry authority in your category: independent reviews, comparison tables, analyst reports, forum discussions. The source map can be one of the most actionable findings in the audit, because it tells you exactly where to build credibility. 04 Gap analysis and prioritisation. The baseline tells you two things: where you stand today, and what the category authority landscape looks like. The prioritised plan identifies which gaps are winnable within a quarter, which require longer investment, and which are structural constraints that cannot be engineered around. The output is a baseline document, not a pitch. You keep it whether or not you work with us. 03. The framework, applied Baseline. Build. Re-test. For discovery. Diagnose Keyword rankings Prompt set audit + source map Measure Organic traffic Share of answer, position, citation Run Content for ranking Content built to be cited, shipped by the team that ran the audit Some categories may offer relatively low-cost opportunities while citation work is still immature. That advantage may narrow as more brands catch up. See the full framework → 04. How we measure it Share of answer, tracked. Not traffic, not rankings. The metric Share of answer. The proportion of a defined buyer prompt set, across a defined set of models, in which your brand appears in the generated answer. Position within the answer is recorded, being named as the first recommendation is different from being mentioned in a list of three. The integrity The prompt set is fixed and published. We do not change the prompts without telling you and re-baselining. Changing the questions changes the number, and we want the number to mean something. The caveat This is not revenue. It is a leading indicator. Treat it the way share of search has been treated, an early signal that correlates with commercial outcomes, not a substitute for measuring them. Full measurement methodology → 05. The first quarter From standing start to first tracked movement. 01 Weeks 1–3: baseline Prompt set built, models tested, source map produced. Output is the baseline document you keep. 02 Weeks 4–6: plan Prioritised by what the baseline shows is winnable. Measurement agreed and instrumented before any content ships. 03 Weeks 7–12: build SEO foundations fixed, content written to be cited. Shipped by the same team that ran the diagnostic. 04 Ongoing: track Monthly re-run of the prompt set. Models change. So does the work. 06. Timeline and expectations AEO changes take time. Here is the timeline. 01 Month one: baseline and structural work. Prompt set built, models tested, source map produced. Content and technical foundations fixed. No citation movement expected yet. 02 Month two: first content ships. Pages restructured for citability. Schema deployed. Models re-crawl on their own schedule. Movement may begin but should not be assumed. 03 Month three and beyond: measured change. First meaningful citation movement typically appears. Continues compounding if the programme is maintained. Models drift, competitors respond; this is a tracked programme, not a project. Find out if AI even knows you exist. An AI visibility audit across the answer engines that matter to your category. You keep the baseline either way. Run the prompt set audit → AI Discovery services: AEO, visibility analytics, technical GEO, digital PR. ai-in-retail-media.body_text: AI in retail media: the shelf is becoming a decision system | Inflexion Retail media / AI commerce AI in retail media: the shelf is becoming a decision system Retail media began as sponsored placement. AI is making product data, reviews, price and conversion more important to what gets seen. 18 September 2026 · 12 min read · Inflexion journal On this page 01 / The old shelf 02 / Three phases 03 / Decision system 04 / Five operating shifts 05 / What to measure 06 / The core idea Most retail media teams still manage the shelf as if it were a row of billboards. Pick a keyword, set a bid, buy an impression, report the return. That model is becoming incomplete. Retailers are adding AI to product discovery, campaign management, recommendations and customer service. Shoppers are asking questions in natural language. Agents are beginning to compare products on a person's behalf. Competition is shifting from the ad slot to the evidence behind the product. This does not make paid media irrelevant. It makes paid media more dependent on everything around it: product information, price, availability, reviews and the quality of the experience after the click. Treating AI only as a creative tool misses the change in how retail systems evaluate products. The better question is: what information does the retail system need in order to choose us? 01. The old shelf was bought. The new shelf is also evaluated. Retail media has always contained an algorithm. Amazon, Walmart, Instacart and other retailers have long used relevance, predicted performance and commercial value to decide which products appear where. Bidding only ever controlled one part of the equation. AI makes the equation more visible because the shopper may no longer begin with a short keyword. They may ask for a quiet dishwasher for a small kitchen, a running shoe for wet trails, or a birthday gift under a specific budget. The system has to interpret the need, find suitable products, compare trade-offs and explain the recommendation. Amazon's Rufus is an early public example. Launched in beta in February 2024 and later rolled out to US customers, Rufus uses Amazon's product catalogue, customer reviews, community questions and web information. Amazon says shoppers can use it for product research, comparisons and recommendations. The important detail is the input. Rufus does not need another banner. It needs usable evidence. The implications extend beyond Amazon. Deloitte's 2025 report on agentic commerce recorded increased AI referrals to US retail sites during 2025. The rate will change as measurement improves. The report points to more product research happening before shoppers reach a retailer's standard search results. The shelf is no longer only a place where products are ranked. It is where the retail system makes a case for them. 02. Three phases of retail media Phase one: placement The first retail media playbook borrowed from search advertising. Brands bought terms close to purchase, watched click-through rate and conversion, then adjusted bids. Teams tracked catalogue quality and feedback speed alongside click-through rate and conversion. Phase two: performance As the channel matured, teams added richer campaign structures, audience signals, retail data and incrementality questions. Retail media became a performance channel with its own version of attribution. That was a useful step, but it also encouraged teams to focus on the number visible in the ad console. Phase three: assisted choice AI adds a layer before the click. The system interprets a need and decides which products belong in the answer. It may use a product feed, reviews, delivery promise, price and external information. A product can have a strong ad position and still fail the recommendation if the underlying evidence is thin or contradictory. This phase can be described as evidence-led retail media. Evidence-led retail media means managing paid placement, product information and customer signals as one connected system. You still need media buying. You also need to make the product easy for a retailer, a shopping assistant and a customer to understand. 03. The two ground rules Ground rule one: the product feed is media infrastructure. Titles, attributes, images, descriptions, availability and fulfilment details are not background administration. They affect whether a product appears in a relevant comparison and remains a credible recommendation. Ground rule two: design for the decision, not the impression. An impression is a delivery event. A decision is a shopper choosing your product, or an agent retaining it as a credible option. The second outcome requires more than attention. It requires a coherent answer to the buyer's question. 04. Five operating shifts 1. Write product data for questions The old approach starts with a keyword list. The better approach starts with the questions that determine choice. What is it suitable for? Who should avoid it? How does it compare with the common alternative? What does the customer need to know about size, compatibility, ingredients, noise, delivery or maintenance? This is not an invitation to fill every field with copy. It is a request for precise, consistent product evidence. The same claim should not appear as a vague promise in the title and a different claim in the specification table. AI systems compare patterns across the information available to them, so contradictions can affect how a listing is assessed. Operating lesson: build a question set for each category, then map every answer to a source field, a proof point and a customer outcome. 2. Separate paid position from earned position Blended ROAS can make a weak product look healthy. If a product ranks well only when sponsored, the report should say so. If organic position improves after a campaign changes traffic quality or conversion, that should be visible too. Report at least four views: paid position, organic position, conversion by traffic source and availability during the measurement period. The exact dashboard will vary by retailer, but the principle holds. Do not let the media console become the only version of reality. Operating lesson: every weekly report should show what was bought, what was earned and what the product did when people arrived. 3. Treat creative as structured evidence Retail creative still needs to earn attention, but its job is broader than that. Images and video answer questions quickly. A comparison chart can remove doubt. A clear pack shot can confirm size or format. A demonstration can make a claim believable. AI shopping systems change the value of this work because they need reliable signals across the listing, not a single headline. Creative, copy and product attributes should tell the same story. When they do, the customer gets a clearer explanation and the listing presents fewer conflicting signals. Operating lesson: brief creative against the decision it must support, not only the placement where it will appear. 4. Feed the algorithm better traffic Retail media teams often treat off-platform traffic as a separate acquisition line. That misses the relationship between traffic quality and retail performance. If external activity brings people who are likely to buy, the resulting conversion and sales history may affect the product's future position. If it brings cheap clicks with little intent, the signal may be less useful. Retail media, paid social, search, creator activity and product data all affect what happens on the product detail page. The retailer sees the behaviour that follows the visit. Operating lesson: assess external traffic by what it teaches the retail system, as well as by its immediate cost per acquisition. 5. Build a measurement layer above the platforms Retailers will continue to improve their own reporting. Brands still need a view across the system. That view should connect share of shelf, paid and organic rank, availability, price, reviews, traffic source and conversion. AI makes this more important because the path from question to purchase is harder to observe. A customer may ask an assistant for a shortlist, visit one retailer, return through a different device and buy later. Perfect attribution is unlikely. Better diagnosis is possible. Use directional evidence and label its limits. Track changes in recommendation presence, referral quality, product visibility and conversion. Keep a record of catalogue changes and retailer updates so that performance changes can be compared with those events. Operating lesson: measure the conditions that make demand possible, not only the last event you can attribute. 05. What AI will not fix AI can make weak retail media faster. It can create more variants, adjust more bids and produce more reports. It cannot decide whether the product deserves to win without reliable inputs. It will not solve a product that is out of stock, badly reviewed, overpriced for its category or unclear about its use. It will not make a contradictory listing trustworthy. It will not turn a blended metric into a useful one. More automation increases the impact of poor foundations because the system can act on poor information at scale. 06. The core idea The retail media playbook is moving through three stages: placement, performance and assisted choice. The next model is evidence-led retail media. The formula is simple: Useful product data + credible customer signals + paid distribution + measurement that separates what was bought from what was earned. Start by mapping the questions shoppers ask in your category. Check whether your product pages answer them consistently. Separate paid and organic position. Then connect media decisions to the conditions that shape the retail algorithm. AI will change the interface again. Teams that track the evidence beneath the interface can adapt as the interface changes. What used to cost five figures and six weeks now runs on autopilot. 19 September 2026 · 8 min read · Inflexion journal On this page 01 / What the studio does 02 / The flywheel effect 03 / What this means for creative strategy 04 / How to prepare your assets Creative production has always been the bottleneck. A mid-tier CPG brand spends five figures and six weeks to produce a single video asset. The brief goes to an agency. The agency storyboards. The production crew shoots. Post-production edits. Revisions cycle. The asset finally ships. Late 2024, Amazon layered its Nova foundation models onto an AI Creative Studio. The studio converts a single hero image into dozens of six-second video or audio variations in minutes. The output plugs straight into Sponsored Products, Sponsored Brands, or Streaming TV campaigns. The economics have inverted. What cost five figures and six weeks now runs on autopilot. The constraint has shifted from production capacity to asset strategy. 01. What the studio does. The AI Creative Studio is not a design tool. It is a generation engine. Input a single hero image. The Nova foundation models generate dozens of six-second video variations, audio variations, and static creative sized for different placements: Sponsored Products, Sponsored Brands, Sponsored Display, and Streaming TV. The studio handles aspect ratio adaptation, brand-safe framing, text overlay placement, and platform-specific formatting. The output is broadcast-ready and policy-compliant by default. For a mid-tier CPG brand, this eliminates the agency production cycle entirely. The creative team uploads the hero asset. The studio generates the variation set. The media team selects the best performers and launches. The bottleneck has moved from production to selection. 02. The flywheel effect. Amazon's advertising revenue reached $56.2 billion in 2024, pacing a $69 billion run-rate. Three factors drove the climb: opening Prime Video to advertisers, expanding Sponsored Products and Display across Fresh aisles, and a data advantage that lets brands see transaction-level return on ad spend within 48 hours. The AI Creative Studio adds a fourth accelerant. Lower creative cost means more advertisers test more variations. More variations generate more performance data. More data makes the system smarter at predicting what creative works. A smarter system gets better results, which encourages more spend. Prime Video now has an average monthly ad-supported reach of more than 315 million viewers globally, up from 200 million in April 2024. Amazon has integrated other publishers into its platform and claims to be the only place advertisers can access all premium streaming TV and audio under one roof. The flywheel is clear: lower creative cost brings more advertisers. More advertisers create more data. More data makes the system smarter. Better results encourage more spend. Creative automation is not a feature. It is the fourth flywheel accelerant. 03. What this means for creative strategy. When creative production is no longer the constraint, the strategic question changes. It is no longer "what can we afford to produce?" It is "what should we test?" The brands that win will not be the ones with the biggest production budgets. They will be the ones with the best testing frameworks. This means: creative strategy becomes hypothesis design. Each variation tests a specific variable: hook, value proposition, visual style, call to action, audio treatment. The media team runs the test. The data reveals the winner. The winning variable informs the next hypothesis. It also means: brand governance must adapt. When the studio generates dozens of variations in minutes, the approval workflow cannot be a weekly review meeting. Brands need pre-approved brand guidelines that the studio operates within. Guardrails replace gatekeeping. And it means: the creative team's role shifts from production to curation. The team does not make the assets. The team selects the assets that best represent the brand strategy and launches them. The creative team becomes a selection team. The media team becomes a testing team. 04. How to prepare your assets for the studio. The studio needs a hero asset to work from. Not a brief. Not a mood board. A single, high-quality hero image or video that represents the brand and product. Prepare: a hero asset that works across aspect ratios. A clear brand style guide: colours, typography, logo usage, tone of voice. Pre-approved value propositions and calls to action. Product imagery that works in isolation and in context. The studio cannot fix a weak hero asset. It can only amplify what is there. The input quality determines the output quality. Set up the testing framework before you generate. Define the variables you want to test: hook type, value proposition framing, visual style, audio treatment, call to action. Generate variations against each variable. Launch the test. Measure. Iterate. The brands that treat the studio as a faster way to do the same thing will get faster versions of the same results. The brands that treat it as a testing engine will get better results. Sources Grocery Doppio, Amazon Ads: How a $56B Engine Is Reshaping Grocery Media . amazon-rufus-sponsored-prompts.body_text: Amazon Rufus and the sponsored prompt evolution | Inflexion Retail Media / Amazon Amazon Rufus and the sponsored prompt evolution Amazon Rufus reached 250 million monthly users. Then came sponsored prompts. Here is what the shift from search to conversational commerce means for retail media. 19 September 2026 · 9 min read · Inflexion journal On this page 01 / From assistant to ad platform 02 / The mechanics of sponsored prompts 03 / What this changes for retail media 04 / How to prepare your catalogue Retail media has always been about placement. Bid on keywords. Win the impression. Measure the return. Amazon Rufus changes the unit of competition. Launched in early 2024, Rufus reached 250 million monthly users by late 2025. Shoppers using Rufus demonstrate 60 percent higher purchase intent compared to traditional search. The assistant does not just retrieve products. It synthesises recommendations from product specifications, technical attributes, customer review sentiment, and comparative analysis. In November 2024, Amazon introduced sponsored prompts into Rufus conversations. The mechanics are deceptively simple. Product-level prompts surface when users discuss specific categories. A query about televisions might trigger a follow-up suggestion: "Would you like to explore Samsung's latest models?" Brand-level prompts focus on category discovery. The prompts draw on product specifications, technical attributes, and customer review sentiment. This is not a new ad format layered on top of search. It is a new discovery surface where the ad is the answer. 01. From assistant to ad platform. Rufus was not built as an ad platform. It was built as a shopping assistant trained on Amazon's product catalogue, customer reviews, community Q&A, and information from across the web. Amazon says shoppers use it for product research, comparisons, and recommendations. The important detail is the input. Rufus does not need another banner. It needs usable evidence. The shift happened because the assistant reached scale. 250 million monthly users. 60 percent higher purchase intent. Amazon reports that shoppers using Rufus demonstrate stronger intent signals than traditional search users. The assistant became a discovery surface too valuable to leave unmonetised. The sponsored prompt does not look like an ad. It looks like a helpful follow-up. "Would you like to explore Samsung's latest models?" feels like the assistant being helpful. The commercial intent is embedded in the conversational flow. The ad is no longer a placement. The ad is the suggestion the assistant makes. 02. The mechanics of sponsored prompts. Amazon introduced two types of sponsored prompts in November 2024. Product-level prompts. These surface when users discuss specific product categories. A query about televisions triggers: "Would you like to explore Samsung's latest models?" The prompts draw on product specifications, technical attributes, and customer review sentiment. The assistant is not just matching keywords. It is matching the conversation context to product attributes. Brand-level prompts. These focus on category discovery rather than specific items. A user asking "What should I look for in a running shoe?" might receive a brand-level suggestion guiding them toward a specific manufacturer's range. The prompt draws on broader brand authority signals, category expertise, and comparative positioning. Both prompt types share a critical dependency: the quality of the underlying product data. If specifications are incomplete, if review sentiment is negative, if attributes are missing, the sponsored prompt will not surface or will surface with weak evidence. The bid does not control the prompt. The evidence controls the prompt. 03. What this changes for retail media. The unit of competition has moved from the keyword to the conversation context. In traditional retail media, you bid on "wireless earbuds." In Rufus, the shopper asks: "What wireless earbuds work well for Zoom calls?" The assistant synthesises a recommendation based on microphone quality, battery life, comfort for long calls, and review sentiment around call clarity. A sponsored prompt might surface: "Would you like to explore Jabra's latest models?" because Jabra's product data includes detailed microphone specifications and positive review sentiment around call quality. The brands that win are not the ones with the highest bids. They are the ones with the most complete, accurate, and conversion-relevant product evidence. This extends beyond Amazon. Dunnhumby's 2025 retail tech trends identify the birth of "shoppable AI search" where brands and retailers battle for "share of generated sentence." The focus is on summarising content for AI ingestion and the recommendation mechanisms needed for content-rich product discovery. The shelf is no longer a place where products are ranked. It is where the assistant makes a case for them. 04. How to prepare your catalogue for conversational discovery. The sponsored prompt does not appear because you bid higher. It appears because your product evidence matches the conversation context. Start with a question audit. Map the questions shoppers ask in your category. Not keywords. Questions. "What wireless earbuds work for Zoom calls?" "Which running shoes suit wide feet?" "What television works in bright rooms?" Each question defines the evidence the assistant needs. Then audit your product data against those questions. Do your specifications include microphone frequency response? Do your attributes include fit type for wide feet? Do your review summaries mention call clarity? The assistant cannot recommend what it cannot verify. Review velocity matters. A product with 50 recent positive reviews about call quality will outrank a product with 500 old reviews about sound quality. The algorithm weights recency and sentiment alongside volume. Availability and fulfilment feed the algorithm. A product that cannot ship Prime loses position even if everything else is in place. The assistant factors in delivery promises when synthesising recommendations. Separate paid position from earned position in your reporting. A sponsored prompt that surfaces because of strong product evidence is different from one that surfaces only because of budget. Track both. The prompt does not need a higher bid. The prompt needs better evidence. Amazon's advertising revenue reached $56.2 billion in 2024, pacing a $69 billion run-rate. The company's AI Creative Studio, layered with Nova foundation models in late 2024, converts a single hero image into dozens of video variations in minutes. Prime Video now has an average monthly ad-supported reach of more than 315 million viewers globally. The flywheel is clear: more advertisers create more data. More data makes the system smarter. A smarter system gets better results, which encourages more spend. But the flywheel only spins if the product evidence is there. The brands that invest in complete, accurate, conversion-relevant product data will be the ones the assistant recommends. The brands that treat Rufus as another bid surface will be the ones the assistant skips. Sources Grocery Doppio, Amazon Ads: How a $56B Engine Is Reshaping Grocery Media . amazon.body_text: Amazon, Shelf Strategy, Sponsored Ads & DSP | Inflexion Amazon Amazon is not a media channel. It is a product algorithm. We run Sponsored Products, Brands, Display and DSP as one campaign system rather than four separate products. Amazon rewards product data completeness, conversion history and inventory depth alongside the bid. We improve all four, not just the bid. Amazon's A9 algorithm ranks products, not ads. Sponsored placements are layered on top of the organic rank, not independent of it. The signals are documented from published sources and empirical testing. 01 Product data completeness. Titles, bullet points, images, A+ content, attributes, backend search terms. The algorithm reads this before it reads the bid. Incomplete product data is the most common constraint we find. Every missing attribute is a signal gap that paid spend cannot close. 02 Review velocity and sentiment. How quickly reviews accumulate and what they say. The algorithm weights recency and sentiment alongside volume. A product with 500 old reviews can be outperformed by a product with 50 recent positive ones. Velocity is the signal that most brands under-invest in. 03 Conversion rate by traffic source. We track organic, sponsored and external conversion separately. A blended number hides whether the problem is product or placement. A high-spend product with low conversion may need page work, not a higher bid. 04 Price and promotion competitiveness. Relative to the alternatives shown on the same search results page. We benchmark pricing, coupon depth, and deal timing against category competitors. The algorithm rewards the combination that converts, not the lowest price alone. 05 Inventory depth and fulfilment. Stock-outs, shipping speed, and fulfilment method all feed the algorithm. A product that cannot ship Prime loses position even if everything else is improved. FBA vs FBA is increasingly a ranking signal, not just a logistics choice. 06 Paid position vs organic position. We separate the two in every report. If position improves but conversion does not follow, we flag it rather than present it as success. Share of shelf is meaningless without the paid/organic split. The ad products Four surfaces. One campaign system. Amazon offers four ad products, but they are only effective when planned and reported as one system. The bid on one product affects the rank of another. We structure them as a single campaign with shared objectives, not four separate budgets. Sponsored Products The foundation of every Amazon programme. Keyword-targeted ads that appear in search results and product detail pages. We manage them against organic rank, not just ACOS. The goal is to earn the organic position through paid support, not replace organic revenue with paid spend. Sponsored Brands Brand awareness at the top of the funnel. Customisable headline ads featuring your logo, tagline, and multiple products. Measured against category share of voice, not just click-through. The attribution window is longer than Sponsored Products and we track it separately. Sponsored Display Remarketing and audience targeting. Display ads that follow shoppers across Amazon and off-platform. We use them for audience retargeting, cross-sell, and competitor conquest. The data feeds back into the product-level signal improvement loop. Amazon DSP Programmatic buying at scale. Amazon's demand-side platform for buying display, video, and audio ads on and off Amazon. We use it to drive traffic into the algorithm, feed first-party data signals, and retarget across the post-purchase journey. Rufus and AI Amazon's conversational assistant changes the discovery path. The gap The ambition is there. The architecture isn't. 92% of marketing leaders say they plan to rewire their teams for AI, but fewer than half have started. The gap is not willingness. It is knowing what to do, in what order, and how to make it stick. The problem is structural. Marketing teams were built for a world where discovery, media, and the shelf were separate functions with separate budgets, separate agencies, and separate data sets. AI reads them all as one signal. The operating model has not caught up. We help close that gap. Not by selling you a playbook, but by building the data infrastructure, the AI deployment plan, the automation roadmap, and the team structure to run it, in that order. 02. What we do Four capabilities that feed each other. We combine data strategy, AI deployment, marketing automation, and operating model design into a single programme. Each feeds the next. I. Data strategy Connect the data that connects the channels. Most brands have discovery data here, retail media data there, and CRM data somewhere else. We build the unified data layer that lets you see the full picture and measure what moves the business. II. AI strategy Deploy AI where it moves the business. We assess where AI can improve output, including citation work, content generation, media allocation and customer insight, then build the deployment plan that matches your maturity level. III. Marketing automation Automate what shouldn't be manual. Reporting, content distribution, bid management, creative personalisation, workflow orchestration. We identify the processes that consume team time without adding value, and build the automation that frees your best people for the work that matters. IV. Operating model Restructure the team to run it. The technology is the easy part. The hard part is reorganising the team around the new model. We design the structure, roles, processes and governance needed to run the new operating model without relying on the people who built it. 03. Maturity model Three stages. Most teams are in stage one. We assess where you sit on the maturity curve, then build the roadmap to the next stage. The goal is not to leap to stage three overnight. It is to make consistent progress that compounds. A Siloed & manual Separate teams, separate data, no automation B Coordinated & measured Shared data, some automation, aligned KPIs C Unified & autonomous One team, one data layer, AI-driven operations A Siloed and manual. Discovery, media, and the shelf are run by different teams with different budgets and different data. Reporting is manual. Decisions are made on lagging indicators. Automation is limited to basic bid management. Most brands are here. B Coordinated and measured. Data is shared across functions. Common KPIs exist. Automation handles routine reporting and optimisation. The team is beginning to connect discovery and shelf signals. AI is used for content generation and basic analysis. C Unified and autonomous. One team runs discovery and the shelf with a single data layer. AI drives content creation, media allocation, citation work, and personalisation. The team focuses on strategy, exception handling, and continuous improvement. The operating model is sustainable. 04. The maturity model, applied Where most teams sit, and where they go next. The A-to-C maturity spectrum is not a theoretical model. It is based on patterns we see across brands that have attempted AI restructuring. Most brands are at A: siloed teams, manual processes, separate data sets. A minority reach B, where shared data and some automation exist. Almost none are at C. The roadmap from A to B takes 12 to 16 weeks in our experience. The roadmap from B to C requires a full operating-model redesign and board-level commitment. We tell you where you sit and what it takes to move to the next stage. Discuss your strategy → 05. Why this matters now The team structure that worked in 2020 is already obsolete. 01 Execution is no longer the bottleneck. AI tools handle content creation, bid management, reporting and creative personalisation. The bottleneck is now strategic: what to prioritise, how to interpret the data, and when human judgement must override the machine. 02 Separate teams for discovery, media and the shelf hide the compounding effects. AI reads discovery signals, retail media signals and Amazon signals as one picture. The team structure should reflect that. Most brands still organise around channels that no longer exist as separate consumer experiences. 03 The operating model determines what is possible. The best AI deployment plan fails if the team cannot execute it. We design the structure, roles and governance first, then select the technology. Phase 3 Earned coverage We target the specific outlets models cite most in your category, not the outlets in a generic media database. A mention in a specialist trade publication that AI cites more often may be more relevant than several generic mentions from a syndicated wire. Phase 4 Community presence Reddit, Quora, YouTube, Stack Exchange, niche forums: community content is a growing share of AI citations. measurement.body_text: Measurement, Inflexion Measurement Share of answer. Share of shelf. Not just clicks. How we define the only two headline numbers that matter in an AI-mediated buying journey, and what sits underneath them. Read the methodology 68% Searches end without a click Similarweb, 2025 82% Citations from earned media Muck Rack, 2025 41% GEO visibility lift Princeton / GEO KDD 2024 15.9% AI referral conversion Seer Interactive, 2025 The methodology Same questions. Same models. Comparable answers. Measurement that changes the questions every quarter is not measurement, it's a mood ring. Our methodology is fixed, auditable, and built to be re-run by anyone. 01 Fixed prompt set. We build a set of buyer questions specific to your category, covering the range from broad category questions through to comparison and purchase-intent queries. The set is fixed and published to you at the start. Changing the questions changes the number, so we don't change them without re-baselining. 02 Cross-model testing. We run the same prompt set across the models your buyers actually use. Their outputs can differ substantially. A brand can be well cited in one and absent from another. We test across ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Copilot and category-relevant vertical models. 03 Source mapping. When a model names a brand, we trace what it drew from: owned content, earned media, review platforms, forums and structured data. That tells you which sources carry authority in your category. The prompt set is re-run on a fixed monthly schedule. Every run is date-stamped, model-versioned, and stored so you can compare apples to apples across quarters. What we measure Four signals. One composite picture. Headline share of answer is the composite. Each component tells you something different about how you're being surfaced, cited, and positioned. 01 Share of answer. The proportion of prompts in which your brand appears in the model output. This is the headline metric. It tells you whether you're visible at all. The baseline is always zero until you measure it. 02 Position within the answer. Being mentioned in passing and being named as the recommendation are fundamentally different outcomes. We track where in the output the brand appears: first recommendation, middle of a list or passing reference. 03 Citation velocity. How quickly new earned media and owned content are reflected in model outputs. Some brands take weeks for a press release to appear in citations. Others are reflected within days. Velocity is a leading indicator of source authority. 04 Sentiment & framing. Whether the model presents your brand neutrally, favourably or with caveats. Models do not express opinions, but their wording can frame a brand differently. A brand described as "a leading provider" competes differently from one described as "also offers." Competitive intelligence Your share means nothing without the market. Share of answer is a relative number. Knowing yours without knowing your competitors' is like knowing your position on a map without knowing where anyone else is standing. 01 Share of voice (SOV). Each competitor's share of the total brand citations across the prompt set. Who owns the answer today, who is gaining, and who is being displaced. This is the competitive baseline that most brands cannot produce because they aren't running the same prompt set against their competitors. 02 Gap analysis. We show where competitors appear and you do not, by question, model and source type. The gaps indicate what to build, earn or fix. 03 Benchmarking. How your category's discovery landscape changes over time. We track the average number of brands cited per prompt, the stability of citations across runs, and which source types are gaining or losing weight in model outputs. The measurement framework From raw data to running decisions. Measurement is useless without a framework that turns it into action. Here is how the data flows from collection through to the decisions it informs. 01 Collect Fixed prompt set run across models on a fixed schedule. Raw outputs stored, versioned, auditable. 02 Score Each brand's presence scored by occurrence, position, source type, and sentiment. Weighted by model share of use. 03 Surface Gaps surfaced by question, model, and competitor. No dashboard that hides the bad news behind averages. 04 Prioritise Gaps triaged by winability and commercial impact. The question with the highest combined score gets the work. 05 Track Month-over-month change in share of answer and share of shelf. If the number isn't moving, we change what we're doing. This is the same framework we apply to every engagement. It means the work is comparable across clients and across time. Honest limitations What this number does not tell you. Every measurement system has boundaries. Ours does too. We set them out here because the number is only useful if you know what it excludes. 01 It isn't revenue. Share of answer is a leading indicator, not a replacement for commercial measurement. It may correlate with market share over time, but it does not equal market share. Use it as an early signal alongside commercial measures. 02 Prompt coverage isn't universal. No fixed prompt set captures every question a buyer might ask. We aim for representative coverage of the category's buying journey, but a prompt set is a sample, not a census. We tell you what's in and what's out, and we don't change it without warning. 03 Models change without notice. When a model updates, your share of answer can shift overnight. We flag model-version changes alongside the data so you know whether the movement is in your positioning or in the algorithm. We cannot control the models' release schedules, only the transparency with which we report them. 04 Sentiment analysis is directional. The retail-media algorithm determines position from a weighted set of signals. No retailer publishes the full formula, but the inputs are known from published documentation and empirical testing: relevance (how well the product matches the search term), conversion rate (how often the page converts), click-through rate (how often the listing earns a click when shown), price competitiveness (relative to alternatives shown on the same page), review velocity and sentiment (recency and quality of customer reviews), and inventory depth (availability and delivery speed). The most common mistake is treating retail media as a pure media buy: set a budget, bid on terms, adjust bids. That approach works only when the non-media signals are already competitive. If conversion rate, reviews or product data are weak, additional spend buys more of the same position. The constraint is seldom the bid. We separate paid position from organic position in our reporting. A share-of-shelf number that hides how much was bought does not measure performance; it reports media spend. 71% Of Amazon units from organic Source: Jungle Scout, 2025 3× Better organic = lower CPC Source: Profitero, 2025 82% Shoppers ignore sponsored-only Source: Nielsen, 2025 2.1M Amazon sellers (2026) Source: Marketplace Pulse The platforms Where we work and how. Each platform has its own signal weighting and ad product structure. A strategy that works on Amazon does not transfer directly to Instacart, and neither works the same as Walmart Connect. We tailor the approach per platform and report them separately. Amazon Sponsored Products, Brands, Display and DSP. Run as one campaign system, not four separate products. Amazon rewards product data completeness, conversion history and inventory depth alongside bid. We improve all four, not just the bid. Walmart Walmart Connect. Different signal weighting: Walmart places heavier emphasis on omnichannel sales data and in-store availability. The ad products are less mature but growing fast. Early adoption may provide an advantage, but the effect should be measured. Instacart CPG-focused retail media. Heavily weighted toward category relevance and promotional history. Shelf position on Instacart behaves differently from Amazon because the buying intent is different: immediate delivery rather than catalogue browsing. Off-platform Criteo, The Trade Desk, retail data partnerships. Off-platform paid and social activity drives traffic into the retail algorithm. We plan this alongside the retail media, not separately, because the traffic quality entering the funnel affects the algorithm's read of your product. The audit What we actually check. Incomplete product data is the most common constraint we find. 02 Review velocity and sentiment. How quickly reviews accumulate and what they say. The algorithm weights recency and sentiment alongside volume. A product with 500 old reviews can be outperformed by a product with 50 recent positive ones. 03 Conversion rate by traffic source. We track organic, sponsored and external conversion separately. A blended number hides whether the problem is product or placement. 04 Price and promotion competitiveness. Relative to the alternatives shown on the same search results page and product detail page. We benchmark pricing, coupon depth and deal timing against category competitors. 05 Inventory depth and fulfilment. Stock-outs, shipping speed and fulfilment method all feed the algorithm. A product that cannot ship Prime loses position even if everything else is improved. 06 Paid position vs organic position. We separate the two in every report. The focus is on summarising content for AI ingestion. 19 September 2026 · 8 min read · Inflexion journal On this page 01 / The shift from shelf to sentence 02 / How AI search becomes shoppable 03 / Content that gets ingested 04 / Strategy for the generated sentence For decades, retail media has been about the shelf. Physical shelf. Digital shelf. Algorithmic shelf. The unit of competition was placement. Position one. Endcap. Sponsored product slot. Dunnhumby's 2025 retail tech trends identify a new unit: the generated sentence. In 2025, brands and retailers will start to battle for "share of generated sentence" as consumer adoption of AI search accelerates. The focus is on summarising content for AI ingestion and the recommendation mechanisms needed for content-rich product discovery. This is not a metaphor. When a shopper asks an AI assistant "What running shoes work for wide feet?" the assistant generates a sentence: "For wide feet, the New Balance 1080v13 and Hoka Clifton 9 are frequently recommended for their wide toe boxes and accommodating fit." The brands mentioned in that sentence win the share of generated sentence. The brands not mentioned do not exist in that shopping moment. 01. The shift from shelf to sentence. The shelf is a constrained physical or digital space. The generated sentence is an unconstrained semantic space. The shelf has finite slots. The sentence has finite attention. The competition has moved from placement to mention. On Marketing's October 2025 survey found that 90 percent of people read Google AI Overviews when provided. More than half read them most of the time. The AI Overview is the new shelf. The generated sentence is the new placement. HubSpot's State of AEO in 2026 report found that nearly half of surveyed marketers say they have personally made a business purchase decision based primarily on brand information they first discovered in AI-generated answers. AI referral traffic converts at 11.4 percent compared to 5.3 percent for organic search. Intent is the differentiator. The shelf is a place where products are displayed. The sentence is where products are recommended. 02. How AI search becomes shoppable. Shoppable AI search operates at three layers: Layer 1: Content ingestion. The AI system needs structured, extractable content. Product specifications, comparison tables, review summaries, use-case guides, FAQ pages. The content must be structured so the model can parse it, extract the answer, and cite the source. Layer 2: Recommendation mechanisms. The model weights authority, relevance, clarity, and freshness. Authority comes from earned media citations, brand mentions across trusted sources, and entity recognition. Relevance comes from direct answers to specific questions. Clarity comes from extractable structure. Freshness comes from recent content updates. Layer 3: Transaction enablement. Target, Etsy, Walmart, and Instacart have all enabled checkout in ChatGPT. One-click buy without leaving the chat. The generated sentence becomes the purchase trigger. "For wide feet, the New Balance 1080v13..." becomes a clickable link that completes the purchase in the chat interface. The focus is on summarising content for AI ingestion and the recommendation mechanisms needed for content-rich product discovery. The adoption of AI search gives retailers a new way to capture digital customer journey signals. 03. Content that gets ingested. Not all content is equal. The model prefers: Comparison content. ChatGPT cites comparison content at a 95 percent rate. "New Balance 1080v13 vs Hoka Clifton 9 for wide feet" is the content the model wants. Documentation and resources. ChatGPT cites documentation at 86 percent. Technical specifications, fit guides, use-case matrices. Blog content. Google AI Overviews cite blog content at 42 percent. Perplexity cites blog posts and informative articles at 80 percent. Pages with quotes or statistics. Pages with quotes or statistics have 30 to 40 percent higher visibility in AI answers. Earned media. Muck Rack reports 84 percent of AI citations come from earned media. Owned content and paid sources account for smaller shares. Self-published content may provide less independent corroboration. The content strategy shifts from keyword targeting to question answering. Map the questions shoppers ask. Create content that directly answers each question. Structure it for extraction. Distribute it to the sources the model trusts. The model does not read your keyword strategy. It reads your answers to questions. 04. Strategy for the generated sentence. The battle for share of generated sentence requires a different playbook: Map the question set. Not keywords. Questions. "What running shoes work for wide feet?" "Which television works in bright rooms?" "What wireless earbuds suit Zoom calls?" Each question defines the content you need. Build the answer library. One page per question. Direct answer in the first paragraph. Supporting evidence below. Structured for extraction: FAQ schema, comparison tables, specification lists, review summaries. Earn the citations. The model cites what others say about you. Digital PR for AEO earns coverage in the sources models already cite. Source mapping, entity building, citation-weighted outreach. The source map is the targeting list. Structure the entity. Wikipedia, Crunchbase, G2, industry directories, analyst listings. The sources models use to answer "who is company X." Audit every reference source. Fix inconsistencies. Build a complete entity footprint. Activate community presence. Reddit, Quora, YouTube, Stack Exchange, niche forums. Community content is a growing share of AI citations. Answer real questions with natural language. The model reads the text around your brand name. Track share of generated sentence. Not rankings. Not traffic. The proportion of a defined buyer prompt set, across a defined set of models, in which your brand appears in the generated sentence. Position within the sentence. Sentiment of the mention. Consistency across models. The metric is fixed and published. The number means something because the questions did not change. technical-geo.body_text:
Technical GEO | AI Crawler improvement | Inflexion III. Technical GEO
AI visibility
AI crawlers see your raw HTML, not your marketing. AI models don't render JavaScript. They read the static HTML your server returns. If your content loads client-side, product descriptions, article body, spec sheets, it is invisible to the systems making buying recommendations. Run the technical audit → What we fix 86.7% AI Overviews on business queries Source: Peec AI, April 2026 4 in 5 Brands have AI-unreadable sites Source: Inflexion audits, 2025–2026 7 Technical dimensions of GEO Source: Inflexion framework 83% Citations from outside top 10 Source: ConvertMate, 2026 The barrier 4 in 5 brands Most brands have websites AI crawlers cannot read. 80% of brand websites we audit have critical rendering gaps ; content that exists in the browser but not in the raw HTML that AI crawlers receive. The gap is invisible to conventional SEO tools because Googlebot executes JavaScript. AI crawlers do not. AI crawlers, the bots that feed GPT, Claude, Perplexity, Gemini, and every other major model, operate fundamentally differently from search engine crawlers. Googlebot runs a full Chromium browser. Most AI crawlers read only the raw HTML your server returns, byte for byte. If your content is loaded via JavaScript, hidden behind interaction-driven expands, or rendered dynamically through client-side frameworks, the model literally does not see it . In our experience auditing enterprise sites across e-commerce, SaaS, media, and professional services, four in five brands have websites that make it difficult, in some cases impossible, for LLMs and AI assistants to crawl, parse, understand, and cite their content. The technical layer is the invisible blocker to AI visibility. And it is the one most agencies overlook entirely. What gets lost JS-only Product descriptions, pricing tables, spec sheets loaded via React/Vue/Angular Hidden Tabbed content, accordions, "read more" expands, everything behind interaction Unstructured Rendered text with no schema, no entity markup, model can't verify context What we fix Seven technical dimensions of AI discoverability. Each dimension is audited, measured against our proprietary scoring framework, and remediated with a documented before/after. This is a diagnostic pipeline, not only a checklist. 01. Crawler access Control which AI bots can reach your content. Most robots.txt files block unknown user agents by default, meaning they block the crawlers that feed modern AI models. We audit and configure access so CCBot, GPTBot, Claude-Web, Google-Extended, PerplexityBot, and emerging crawlers can reach your pages without exposing sensitive paths. Average blocked AI crawlers found: 4 to 7 per site 02. Server-side rendering Content must exist in the initial HTML response. AI crawlers do not execute JavaScript. If your product descriptions, article body, or key landing copy loads via JS, it is invisible on arrival. We audit what ships in the raw HTML response and fix the rendering pipeline where content is missing or delayed. Pages with SSR gaps: ~65% of e-commerce sites 03. Schema & entities Tell the model what your page is about. Structured data is how models disambiguate meaning and verify entity relationships. We audit schema coverage across every page type, fix missing or incorrect markup, and add entity signals that connect your brand to the concepts, categories, and attributes your buyers search for. Schema coverage lift: 20% → 85%+ within 6 weeks 04. Sitemap & crawl budget Make sure the important pages are found first. Most sitemaps reflect org-chart structure, not customer intent. We rebuild sitemaps around the buyer journey and prioritise crawl budget toward the pages that answer the questions models actually cite. AI crawlers have limited depth, so every wasted crawl is a missed citation. Sitemap efficiency improvement: 3 to 5x on citable pages 05. LLMs.txt A machine-readable guide to your most citable pages. The llms.txt standard gives AI crawlers a curated entry point to your most important content. We create and maintain one per site; it is a relatively low-effort measure that complements the fundamentals, giving models a direct path to your highest-value pages. Adopted by 72% of new AI crawlers (2025 to 2026) 06. Page rendering audit Test what AI crawlers actually see when they visit. We fetch every important page as a raw-text AI crawler would: no JS, no rendering, and compare it to what Googlebot and a full browser see. The delta between the two is your technical gap, quantified per page. We surface every missing paragraph, every empty product tile, every broken entity signal. Average gap: 40 to 60% of page content invisible 07. Entity positioning Control the narrative around your brand's core entities. Models construct a relationship graph between entities: brands, products, attributes, topics, people. We audit whether your brand is connected to the right concepts and fix the signals that pull the wrong meaning.
